text: Olive drab. It's the color on almost every American bomb and artillery shell, and on its own, it means almost nothing.
It's the base coat. Under the military's ammunition color code, mil standard seven oh nine, the real message is painted on top, as a stripe.
That code covers ammunition twenty millimeters and larger. Smaller bullets use a different system, a painted tip.
Yellow. A yellow band means high explosive.
A live Mark eighty-two, the five hundred pound general purpose bomb, is olive drab with a yellow band about three inches wide around the nose.
Bombs with a heat resistant thermal coating get two yellow bands. One stripe, and everyone on the flight line knows. This one is real.
Brown. Brown means low explosive.
Not the blast, the push. Propellant charges and rocket motors. A low explosive burns very fast instead of detonating.
So a brown band on a missile tells the crew loading it that the motor is live, even if the warhead isn't.
Light blue. Light blue means practice.
The B D U thirty-three is a blue, twenty-five pound practice bomb built to fly like a Mark eighty-two.
But blue does not mean harmless. Inside is a spotting charge that throws up a puff of smoke, so crews can score their hit.
There are hundreds of thousands of them on American bombing ranges, and the Air Force's advice if you find one is simple. Don't pick it up.
Light green. Light green means smoke.
Screening smoke, to hide troops and vehicles. Or marking smoke, to point out a target or a landing zone. This round is built to hide things, not to destroy them.
White. White means illumination.
These rounds aren't meant to hit the ground. High above the battlefield, the shell releases a flare that drifts down under a parachute and turns the night bright.
Black. Black means armor defeating.
These are the rounds built to punch through tanks. It's the same idea as the black tip on an armor piercing bullet.
And gray. Gray is the one nobody wants to see. A gray body means chemical.
The band tells you which kind. Dark red is a riot control agent, like tear gas. Violet is an incapacitating agent. Dark green is a toxic chemical.
And if that dark green band is broken into half inch dashes, it marks a binary nerve agent. Two chemicals stored apart, that only mix after the round is fired.
Colors fade, and other countries use their own codes, so a color is never proof that something is safe.
But on an American flight line, yellow is the blast, brown is the push, blue is practice, green is smoke, white is light, black is armor, and gray is the one you hope never leaves the bunker.
Which stripe surprised you the most? Tell me in the comments.
